market_context: United States; FDA nutrient-content claims and Nutrition Facts labeling
title: Low Fat, Reduced Fat, or Fat-Free: What Actually Changes

seo.title: Low Fat vs Reduced Fat vs Fat-Free
seo.meta_description: On U.S. labels, fat-free generally means less than 0.5 g fat per serving, low fat means 3 g or less per reference amount, and reduced fat means at least 25% less than a reference food.
seo.search_intent: Explain the U.S. labeling difference between fat-free, low-fat, and reduced-fat claims.

excerpt: These claims answer different questions. “Fat-free” and “low fat” use absolute limits, while “reduced fat” compares the product with a reference version and requires at least 25% less fat.
content_html:
A yogurt marked “reduced fat” can still contain more fat than a different yogurt marked “low fat.” The reason is that U.S. labeling rules use two different systems: absolute thresholds for “fat-free” and “low fat,” and a comparison rule for “reduced fat.”

Fat-free is the strictest absolute claim

Under FDA rules, “fat-free” generally means less than 0.5 gram of total fat per reference amount and labeled serving. It does not mean a mathematically perfect zero; label rounding and the legal threshold matter.

Low fat uses a higher fixed ceiling

For most individual foods, “low fat” means 3 grams of fat or less per reference amount, with additional rules when the reference amount is very small. Meals and main dishes use a per-100-gram criterion and a limit on the share of calories from fat.

Reduced fat is a comparison with another food

“Reduced fat” generally requires at least 25% less fat than an appropriate reference food. That can still leave a substantial amount of fat if the regular version was high in fat to begin with. A reduced-fat cheese, for example, is not automatically a low-fat cheese.

The Nutrition Facts panel settles the practical question

Use the front claim to understand what rule the product meets, then compare grams of total fat and serving size on the Nutrition Facts panel. Reduced describes the change; low and free describe the amount.

faq.question: Does fat-free mean zero grams of fat?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. FDA generally allows the claim when the food contains less than 0.5 g per reference amount and labeled serving.

faq.question: How much less fat does reduced fat mean?
faq.answer: Generally at least 25% less fat than an appropriate reference food.

faq.question: Can reduced-fat food still be high in fat?
faq.answer: Yes. A 25% reduction from a high-fat reference food can still leave more than the amount allowed for a low-fat claim.
